975.q: If anything — and I have had a number of students over the years, some stride students who want to learn how to do that because it’s just something that’s so old that very few people do it anymore. Although there’s a wave of young players coming up right now who are fascinating for that very…

220.t: Etudes, tension and release, and silence in music
220.s: Etudes are not music; good music is tension and release, with silence important; musicianship cannot be taught, only encouraged.
220.q: No, they’re etudes. And etudes are studies and that’s what they were meant to be, and that’s what they are. Because you can’t consider most etudes as music, because they’re not. You know they were designed to do a certain thing. Technically you know. But you know most students, they spend so much…

983.t: Teaching at the New School and the loss of places to hear live jazz
983.s: He describes students after school, the lost Birdland and Jazz Gallery era, and says the music will survive like a roach.
983.q: There hasn’t been too much. There hasn’t been a replacement. In fact I teach at the New School. I’ve been there about six or seven years I guess. Maybe seven or eight years. And it’s very interesting to see what happens semester after semester. The great thing about the New School at first, and…

612.t: Advice for young players; teaching by ear near Nashville
612.s: He describes the by-ear violin school where he will teach.
612.q: Well in a few days I’ll be down about 40 miles from Nashville. There’s a place down there where there’s something like 150 or 200 young violinists go twice a year to study violin. And it’s by ear. I mean, not notes you know. So this will be my first year down there to teach them. And we heard…

906.t: Learning jazz in schools versus on the road
906.s: They discuss how jazz was once learned by listening and playing in bands, while students now study it in courses and seminars with few chances to perform.
906.q: Like you have to feel it. Because I’m sure when Clark Terry was coming up there were no courses in jazz. But now you go to school to learn jazz.

477.t: Students' unfamiliar methods and the pivot system
477.s: He asks students to explain approaches he does not know, and recalls the upstream/downstream pivot system teacher and Berklee's trombone numbers.
477.q: Well I would answer them with an inquiry if I had never heard of that approach I would ask to have the student explain what was involved. And I was trying to think of an example of that and I suppose — it wasn’t Remington, Remington was a great teacher, no, no, no — Philadelphia — damn. There was a…

552.t: Jazz education and the oral tradition
552.s: Musicians joining education, but the oral tradition and folk core of the music matter.
552.q: Yeah. Yeah I think fortunately, now I’ve seen the trend in the last ten years where more of the street musicians have gotten involved, musicians that are in the scene, of the scene, in addition to educators. And I think that’s been a positive. I think Bunky Green had a lot to do with that when he…

469.t: How the music was learned then versus in schools now
469.s: Learning by watching and listening, with no jazz classes or books then.
469.q: Yeah absolutely. You’re right, you’re right. And there’s some great, great schools and there are great programs now, music programs that we didn’t have. We didn’t have access to it. Rick, I don’t know, you know well I mean I’m older than you so, but I don’t remember jazz classes and stuff like that.

449.s: Rowe sympathizes with university jazz programs needing methodology.
449.q: We’re going to learn everything and then forget it and just blow you know.

153.s: Brown laments students lacking the humanity of the music; Bellson agrees, citing the Rendezvous apprenticeship, Pearl's 'join the club' and Fred Astaire learning to walk.
153.q: That’s a good analogy. I go way back to when me and the Rendevous Club with a quartet. I played with them every Tuesday night. After I did that for two or three years, I was ready to go join Benny Goodman’s band. I was ready to swing, because I knew what swing was all about. I knew what was playing…

368.t: Eddie Daniels, and his students Ronnie Aldrich and Steve Botek
368.s: He praises Eddie Daniels and explains why he taught only two people.
368.ch: Later life, Terry Gibbs and Artie Shaw
368.q: Yeah, my disciples. Well, I kind of take the credit for discovering, partially discovering, Eddie Daniels. That’s when he was with the Thad Jones—Mel Lewis band. He’s one of the best I’ve ever heard on it.

142.t: Young musicians crossing worlds and a general music education
142.s: More young players move between jazz and classical; he would teach both groups together, giving everyone a general music grounding as Gunther Schuller proposed.
142.q: More and more. More and more; thank God. That’s happening little by little, but it is, it took years, and still some people, they don’t want to close the deal inside. They are afraid of something, I don’t know. It’s like some people have a block about reading music; it’s the same thing.

110.t: Teaching a jazz extension course with Iola; Herb Wong
110.s: Iola lectured while Dave played examples in a Berkeley extension class that included young Herb Wong.
110.ch: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
110.q: So we got to know Herb really well, and of course we work with him all the time at Monterey now. We’re old friends. Then we moved over to San Francisco extension.

86.t: Never taught privately; the Duke Ellington Fellowship at Yale
86.s: He has visited schools but never taught lessons, despite his Ellington Fellowship.
86.q: No, never have. I’ve often wanted to but nobody ever approached me, so consequently, I’ve never gone out and hung my shingle out, “Trumpet Lessons.”

491.t: How jazz schools have changed the music
491.s: Golson says early jazz programs produced stiff players, but later teachers who could actually play prepared students better, though success still depends on the individual and on getting out to play.
491.ch: Advice, education and the evolution of jazz
491.q: Not in the beginning, but now, to a certain extent. It’s not a totality. Because in the beginning, when they started to have these schools, when – it started to happened when the men came home from the Vietnam – um . . .

135.t: The Lenox School of Jazz and the Music Barn
135.s: Heath describes the MJQ as artists-in-residence, the school's faculty, his student Larry Ridley, and why the school ended.
135.ch: Films, Lenox and tensions with Milt
135.q: We became the artists-in-residence or something like that at the Music Barn, and they had erected a nice tent there to accommodate these concerts, but we were there all summer. By being artists-in-residence we did two or three concerts during the summer. The idea came to John to have a school up…

651.t: Other jazz camps and band directors' weak ears
651.s: More camps now exist but are not like his; he thinks average band directors lack ear training, and describes splitting theory classes by level.
651.q: It’s an economic challenge. But I also realize that those camps are nothing like our camps. Nothing at all. We say “for the serious musician.” I think those camps often feel like... The people running those camps at the college level, I think they often feel like our camp would be over the heads of…

451.q: That was the cover of a CD, right. Parenthetically again, he did all that stuff. He never charged me a cent for anything and he’s this expensive, famous cartoonist and he would just do these things. I would have to hear it again, but I imagine it has some relationship to Gary. And it was a way of…

108.s: He gave up teaching because of unpredictable studio calls.
108.q: Some years ago I did. I taught a couple kids. At that time I was very busy. So when you’d have a lesson scheduled for today at two o’clock, and the night before, I would get a call at eleven o’clock at night, a jingle date or something at two, I’d have to call and say, “You can’t come today.” So I…

225.t: Teaching: Oberlin residency, Indiana State and Ball State
225.s: Clinics, the Danenberg residency at Oberlin and contracts with Indiana State and talks with Ball State.
225.q: Uh huh. My first exposure in that area of endeavor was the National Association of Jazz Educators. A few years ago they held their annual bash [conference] in Detroit, and Mary Ann Topper managed to get me involved in a situation. I was one of the guest performers and clinicians at that meeting of…

686.t: Role as an educator and respect for older generations
686.s: He talks about elders in his family, preserving the older musicians' work, and being both reverent and irreverent toward repertory.
686.q: We grew up with older people in our lives: my great uncle, who I used to hang out with. I was 8, and he was 86 or 87. I learned a lot from he and his wife, my Aunt Marguerite.

408.s: Teaching, music lessons and being a cultured person.
408.q: I’m all for it, I mean anything that puts an instrument in the kid’s hands is, he’s less likely to buy an Uzi and shoot me. [both chuckle] No I think I mean that I think learning an instrument makes you a better citizen, makes you no matter what you decide to do in life, I think having some music…

123.t: Clubs versus concerts, local artists and university ties
123.s: They discuss club residencies, local players weekdays, and ties with Roosevelt, Columbia and DePaul.
123.ch: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
123.q: During the week, yeah. During the week we charge a lot less and of course we have to pay a lot less. But we pay them a nice wage, you know, and they come in. And there’s a lot of great local people. And actually we’re going to start featuring them more on the weekends too, come next year, so we…

509.t: Why she is a poor teacher
509.s: She has no patience for teaching singers, and recalls bad piano teachers.
509.q: No. I had a friend that I helped out, but no, I‘m not a good teacher at all, and I found that out when my daughter would play piano.

367.t: Why the touring big bands trained better musicians
367.s: Young laments that today's players lack big-band road schooling and he and Brown list bands like Basie, Hines and Andy Kirk.
367.q: You see what I‘m…but that‘s the reason though, you know. I don‘t think, it‘s too bad that they don‘t have a situation like that now where they have big bands and a lot musicians go out and play in them bands and get the knowledge of playing music because they don‘t have, I don‘t think they have…

109.t: Teaching at the Conservatoire Saint-Germain and its dropping of jazz
109.s: He taught five years at a municipal conservatory, growing it from four to 89 students, until the director dropped jazz hoping for national status and then asked him back.
109.ch: Faith, Paris life and later years
109.q: Uh-huh. And then I opened -- we opened our own school and all that. But it's things -- you know, what happened at the Conservatoire Saint Germain-Orleans was a funny thing. Which they were going to be nationalized, which meant that the state was going to pay for everything.

406.t: Teaching a summer jazz class at Pratt in the riot years
406.s: A group of about ten musicians taught underprivileged children in a building donated at Pratt one summer under Mayor Lindsay's administration.
406.q: But in '68 then I went back to play with Don Ewell at the Golden Nugget in Toronto, and then -- and then I started going to the Poconos -- and then we had a group that taught school for -- out in Pratt University for the summer, for the summer session, and I think --

1.t: Danny's gigs, the Fairview Baptist church band and traditional New Orleans music
1.s: Danny teaches kids traditional music with Lucien and Charlie Barbarin at Fairview Baptist, says Dixieland was a name whites gave to New Orleans music, and notes musicians play until they die.
1.ch: Cab Calloway's band, Hadacol and closing reflections
1.q: Yeah. I have some kids I've been working with the last nine years. The Fairview Baptist Church Christian(?) Band, which is kids who are musically inclined, and Lucien and me and Charlie Barbarin, we have two sons... That's mostly why I got involved with it. Lucien and Charlie Barbarin, we were…

230.t: Kenton, Herman and Basie touring, and young college-trained players
230.s: Barnet recounts seeing Basie at the ballpark and Kenton and Herman's high costs, and says college bands are precise but their soloists are plastic.
230.ch: Retirement and the future of big bands
230.q: I've got the place here in San Diego and the boat, and I've got my home in Palm Springs and this is just fine, because we get the same bands here in San Diego that appear in Los Angeles, and they're a lot more accessible here. Like Stan Kenton has been here, and Woody Herman, Harry James, Count…

17.t: Local work and clinics at Capital
17.ch: Life in Columbus and recent activity
17.q: Oh yeah, I do several little clinics, several little seminars with the jazz arts group. Then with the small group and of course the jazz arts group is the big band, and the fusion band. I did a couple of little things there with them, you know.

106.t: Teaching at the Cercle Culturel de Saint-Gratien
106.s: For eighteen years he has taught trumpet, saxophone and drums three days a week at a music school and received a city medal; he is nearly 81.
106.q: So, it made me 66. And I went out to -- but before I retired, I went out to -- I was passed out to this conservatory, where I'm at, actually --

93.s: Asked why masters no longer have protégés, Green says dancers do not fraternise, the woman interviewer suggests schools, and Green names Jimmy Slyde and Sandman Sims as teachers.
93.q: Well, that's because they don't buddy-buddy. They don't fraternize enough with -- well, there's one that does it. I think he's -- what did -- George Nuremberg, that's Nipsy Russell's protégé. Sandman. I think he has done this, Sandman Sims, see. Because -- do you understand? He is a Hooper, you…

29.s: Howard says he taught many students but none made it big because they wanted to play jazz rather than study.
29.q: No, they never got to be in the big time. They wouldn't listen to you. They didn't want to play that. Tell you in a minute, listen, you come on and play some jazz with us.

454.t: A real school of jazz: faculty, students and Paul Jeffries
454.s: Mingus says the music is taught mainly to white players, names ideal teachers, and says composition cannot be taught.
454.ch: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
454.q: I would have Sonny Rollins, Buddy Colette, somebody who could teach classical fundamentals, as well as jazz improvisation.

96.q: That's right. (LAUGHTER). That's right. That's right. But when I took up music boy, I stopped being a bum. I had to devote all my time to that horn.

168.t: Faculty position at Binghamton State University
168.s: From 1969-70 he has been part-time faculty, bringing jazz musicians for concerts and workshops.
168.q: Well, at the time -- this is a part-time situation, where it's not a steady thing. I'm just on the faculty and every once in a while, I have given concerts, you know, and what do you call them? Student affairs, like I played and brought in many, many names in jazz to the university and what have…

19.t: Bill Harris's Pig Foot workshop and young talents
19.s: As musical director he runs a workshop whose young musicians include George Johnson, tied to Eddie Jefferson and James Moody, and singer Rod Willoughby.
19.ch: Al Hibbler, Dakota Staton and later years
19.q: I had a beautiful experience in a club that Bill Harris, the guitarist that was with the group called The Clovers for quite a long time, as a matter of fact, the extent of their career... Bill Harris opened a club here, and he called it the Pig Foot. I was asked to come in and be musical director…

78.t: Plan to let high-school stage bands play Horace's and Fletcher's arrangements
78.s: The interviewer suggests school big bands could perform historical charts; Horace agrees to bring arrangements and they discuss instrumentation and extra parts.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: You know, Tom, I'm looking forward to that. I would like to bring out some of the arrangements even that were made back in those days, because some of them are still modern. That's how far ahead -- (unintelligible).

529.t: Is jazz ever dead; disc jockeys and jazz teaching in schools
529.s: Sam says jazz has never died, blames uninformed disc jockeys, and welcomes jazz musicians teaching in schools.
529.q: Exactly, that's what it is, you know. And then you got, the, the, like I say, you got disc jockeys on the air, man, push--they don't know any better. If they know, if...there are disc jockeys that that knew better, they aren't there any more. They was fired, or either they quit. So disc jockeys…

112.t: Why he quit teaching in Wilmington
112.s: Wooding quit after classes of forty with few serious students and a principal telling him not to bother teaching music reading.
112.q: I was teaching Clifford Brown in '45 and '46 and going into '47. Then I got sick of it. I got sick of it down there because when you're teaching in those schools, nowadays, you have 40 in a class. But only 5 of them want music. The rest of them want recreation. And they come in the class and…
